title: Venepuncture, blood results and ECGs
blurb: Take blood samples that give true results, act promptly on abnormal bloods, and record a 12-lead ECG correctly.
question: Mrs Lowe, 80, takes ramipril and spironolactone. The laboratory phones a potassium of 6.7 mmol/L; the sample was not haemolysed. She feels well. What should the nurse do?

teach.h: A result is only as good as the sample
teach.body: Routine investigations, such as blood tests and ECGs, are part of nursing assessment: the NMC expects you to undertake them, interpret the findings, share them and act promptly, escalating when required. Formally, the pre-analytical phase is everything before the laboratory test: identification, technique, labelling and transport. In plain English: a badly taken sample can produce a frightening number that is not real, or hide one that is.
teach.cite: NMC proficiencies P3.11, P3.12, Annexe B 2.2–2.3

teach.h: Taking a sample that tells the truth
items: Identify the person positively and explain the procedure; gain consent.
Choose an arm without an IV infusion or cannula in use, and avoid any haematoma.
Apply the tourniquet for no longer than 1 minute; ask the person not to clench or pump the fist, which can falsely raise potassium.
Clean with 70% alcohol and let it dry; use a suitable needle size, as too small a needle can damage cells.
Label every tube in the presence of the person, at the bedside, with the time of collection.

children.label: Tell the doctor; repeat the sample promptly

teach.caption: Haemolysis, a long tourniquet time and fist clenching or pumping can falsely raise potassium. Never assume a result is false without telling the doctor and repeating it.

teach.caption: NICE NG253: in suspected sepsis at high risk, take a venous blood gas (with glucose and lactate), blood culture, FBC, CRP, U&E, creatinine, LFTs and clotting.

head: Electrode
Position
rows: Anterior axillary line, level with V4
Mid-axillary line, level with V4 and V5
teach.caption: Find the angle of Louis, slide down to the 2nd intercostal space and count down. Common errors: V1 and V2 placed too high, V4–V6 too low.

teach.h: Limb electrodes (proximal to wrists and ankles)
teach.caption: A memory aid: 'Ride Your Green Bike' clockwise from the right arm.

teach.body: Position the person semi-recumbent at about 45 degrees, relaxed and warm, with dignity preserved: muscle tension causes artefact. Prepare the skin if needed. When breast tissue covers the correct positions, the convention is to place V4–V6 beneath the left breast. Check the trace has a stable baseline and clear P, QRS and T waves. Write any symptoms at the time, such as chest pain, on the ECG, document any change from standard positions, and bring urgent features to the attention of appropriate staff straight away.
teach.cite: SCST Clinical guidelines: recording a standard 12-lead ECG (2024)

teach.h: Worked example: Mr Abbott's chest pain on a surgical ward
items: Mr Abbott, 67, calls with central chest tightness. The nurse assesses ABCDE and calls for help: RCUK advises an early 12-lead ECG for suspected acute coronary syndrome.
She sits him at about 45 degrees, places the electrodes using the landmarks and records the trace.
He says the pain is still present, so she writes 'chest pain during recording' and the time on the ECG.
She shows the ECG to the doctor immediately rather than filing it, and prepares for bloods as requested.

teach.text: V1 and V2 sit in the 4th intercostal space, not the 5th: V4 is the one in the 5th. And a haemolysed high potassium is neither ignored nor simply treated: tell the doctor and repeat the sample promptly.

items: Avoid the infusion arm; tourniquet no longer than 1 minute; no fist clenching or pumping; label at the bedside.
Haemolysis and poor technique can falsely raise potassium: report and repeat.
Lactate over 2 mmol/L in medium-risk sepsis means treat as high risk (NICE NG253).
Chest electrodes: V1/V2 4th space either side of sternum, V4 5th space mid-clavicular, V5/V6 level with V4.
Limb leads: red right arm, yellow left arm, green left leg, black right leg.

summary: You can now take blood samples in a way that gives reliable results, recognise when a result may be false, and escalate abnormal results such as high potassium or lactate promptly. You can place 12-lead ECG electrodes correctly and record, annotate and share a trace safely.

A.q: Where should the V1 electrode be placed when recording a 12-lead ECG?
options: 4th intercostal space, left sternal edge
5th intercostal space, mid-clavicular line
4th intercostal space, right sternal edge
2nd intercostal space, right sternal edge
A.why: SCST: V1 (red, C1) goes in the 4th intercostal space at the right sternal edge.

whyNot.0: The 4th space at the left sternal edge is V2.
whyNot.1: The 5th space in the mid-clavicular line is V4.
whyNot.3: The 2nd space is used as a landmark for counting down; placing V1 this high is a common error.

A.q: During venepuncture, for how long should the tourniquet ideally remain in place?
options: No longer than 1 minute
Up to 3 minutes
Until every tube is filled
Up to 5 minutes
A.why: Tourniquet application should not exceed 1 minute, because longer times cause haemoconcentration and haemolysis that distort results.

whyNot.1: Three minutes is long enough to cause haemoconcentration and falsely altered results.
whyNot.2: The tourniquet should be released once blood flow is established, not left on while all tubes fill.
whyNot.3: Five minutes would significantly affect results such as potassium.

A.q: Why should blood not be taken from an arm with an intravenous infusion running?
options: The infusion makes the veins collapse
Infusion fluid can contaminate the sample
It increases the risk of a vasovagal faint
The tourniquet would trigger the pump alarm
A.why: Blood from an arm with IV access can be contaminated by the infusion fluid, giving erroneous results, and has a higher risk of haemolysis.

whyNot.0: An infusion does not make veins collapse; the concern is contamination of the sample.
whyNot.2: Fainting risk depends on the person, not on which arm is used.
whyNot.3: Pump alarms are not the reason; inaccurate results are.

B.q: When applying the limb electrodes for a 12-lead ECG, which colour goes on the left leg?
options: Black
Yellow
Red
Green
B.why: SCST: left leg (LL) is green; right arm red, left arm yellow, right leg black.

whyNot.0: Black is the right leg electrode.
whyNot.1: Yellow is the left arm electrode.
whyNot.2: Red is the right arm electrode.

B.q: Mr Shah, 61, has suspected sepsis from a urinary infection and a NEWS2 of 6. His venous lactate is 3.1 mmol/L. How should he be managed under NICE NG253?
options: Defer antibiotics for up to 3 hours as medium risk
Repeat the lactate in 4 hours before deciding
Treat as high risk, with antibiotics within 1 hour
Manage as low risk, as lactate is under 4 mmol/L
B.why: NG253 rec 1.8.20: a person at medium risk with evidence of hypoperfusion, such as lactate over 2 mmol/L, should be treated as if at high risk, including IV antibiotics within 1 hour.

whyNot.0: Deferral is an option for medium risk without hypoperfusion; a lactate over 2 changes this.
whyNot.1: Waiting 4 hours delays high-risk treatment that NICE says should start within 1 hour.
whyNot.3: The NG253 hypoperfusion marker is lactate over 2 mmol/L, not 4.

B.q: Which position does SCST guidance recommend for recording a standard 12-lead ECG?
options: Sitting fully upright at 90 degrees
Semi-recumbent at about 45 degrees
Lying on the left side
Standing with arms by the sides
B.why: SCST recommends a semi-recumbent position of about 45 degrees, with the person relaxed to avoid artefact from muscle tension.

whyNot.0: Sitting fully upright increases muscle tension and is not the standard position.
whyNot.2: Lying on the side changes the heart's position relative to the electrodes.
whyNot.3: Standing causes muscle artefact and risks falls.

C.q: Mrs Lowe, 80, takes ramipril and spironolactone. The laboratory phones a potassium of 6.7 mmol/L; the sample is not haemolysed. She feels well. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Withhold ramipril and recheck with tomorrow's bloods
Inform the doctor now and record a 12-lead ECG
Document it, as she has no symptoms at present
Ask the laboratory to recheck the same sample later
C.why: A potassium over 6.5 mmol/L is severe hyperkalaemia (RCUK 2025) and needs urgent medical review; an ECG shows whether there are changes that need immediate treatment. Acting promptly on results is a patient safety proficiency (P3.12).

whyNot.0: Waiting until tomorrow delays treatment of a potentially life-threatening result.
whyNot.2: Severe hyperkalaemia can cause arrhythmias without warning symptoms.
whyNot.3: The sample is not haemolysed; delaying escalation to recheck it is unsafe.

C.q: While a nurse is recording Mr Abbott's 12-lead ECG, he says his chest pain has come back. What should she do with the trace?
options: Repeat the ECG once his pain has settled
File it in the notes for the ward round
Note the pain on it and show the doctor now
Remove the chest leads and start again
C.why: SCST: symptoms of possible cardiac origin at the time of recording must be noted on the ECG, and features needing urgent attention brought to appropriate staff straight away.

whyNot.0: A trace during pain is valuable; waiting may lose the changes it shows.
whyNot.1: Filing delays review of a possibly urgent ECG.
whyNot.3: Restarting loses a trace recorded during symptoms and delays review.

C.q: Ms Grant, 55, needs a 12-lead ECG. Breast tissue overlies the correct V4 position. What does SCST guidance describe as the convention?
options: Place V4–V6 over the breast tissue
Move V4–V6 up one intercostal space
Leave out V4–V6 and record limb leads
Place V4–V6 beneath the left breast
C.why: SCST: by convention V4, V5 and V6 are placed beneath the left breast when breast tissue overlies the anatomical positions, with care and sensitivity (for example lifting with the back of the hand).

whyNot.0: Placing electrodes on breast tissue is not the current convention, although evidence is still being gathered.
whyNot.1: Moving electrodes up a space changes the recording and is a recognised error.
whyNot.2: A 12-lead ECG needs all chest leads; omitting them gives an incomplete trace.

reteach.title: Ask: is it real, and who needs to know?
reteach.question: Every abnormal result raises two questions. What are they, and in what order?

blocks.body: First, could the result be false? Think about the sample: haemolysis, a drip arm, a long tourniquet, fist clenching or pumping. Second, whatever the answer, who needs to know now? A possibly false potassium of 6.7 still goes to the doctor, with a prompt repeat. A genuine one goes to the doctor urgently with an ECG.

blocks.text: Electrode colours: V1 red, V2 yellow, V3 green, V4 brown, V5 black, V6 purple. Limb: red right arm, yellow left arm, green left leg, black right leg.

explain.body: Avoid the infusion arm and haematomas, keep the tourniquet on no longer than 1 minute, ask the person to keep the hand open and not to clench or pump the fist, clean with 70% alcohol and let it dry, and label in the person's presence.

test.q: During venepuncture, what should the nurse ask the person to do with their hand?
options: Open and close the fist repeatedly
Keep the fist clenched until the draw ends
Squeeze a ball for 2 minutes
Keep the hand open, without clenching
test.why: EFLM-COLABIOCLI venous blood sampling recommendation 6.5: warn the patient not to clench or pump the fist, because both can cause pseudohyperkalaemia and alter other results; the fist should be open when blood flows (9.4).

whyNot.0: Repeated pumping raises some analytes and distorts results.
whyNot.1: Keeping the fist clenched during the draw can also falsely raise potassium; EFLM says the fist should be open when blood flows.
whyNot.2: Prolonged squeezing has the same effect as pumping and can cause pseudohyperkalaemia.

explain.body: Haemolysis (from a small needle, forcing blood through a syringe, a long tourniquet time or a drip arm) can falsely raise potassium. Report it, and repeat the sample promptly.

test.q: What effect can haemolysis of a blood sample have on the potassium result?
options: It can falsely raise it
It can falsely lower it
It has no effect on it
It stops it being measured
test.why: Red cells contain a lot of potassium; when they break open in the tube, the measured potassium can be falsely high.

whyNot.1: Haemolysis releases potassium from cells, so it raises rather than lowers the result.
whyNot.2: Haemolysis is a well-recognised cause of falsely high potassium.
whyNot.3: The laboratory can usually still measure it but will flag haemolysis.

explain.body: V1 4th space right sternal edge; V2 4th space left sternal edge; V4 5th space mid-clavicular line; V3 midway between V2 and V4; V5 anterior axillary line and V6 mid-axillary line, level with V4.

test.q: Where is the V4 electrode placed?
options: 4th intercostal space, left sternal edge
5th intercostal space, mid-clavicular line
5th intercostal space, mid-axillary line
4th intercostal space, anterior axillary line
test.why: SCST: V4 (brown, C4) is in the 5th intercostal space in the mid-clavicular line.

whyNot.2: The mid-axillary line, level with V4, is V6.
whyNot.3: V5 is on the anterior axillary line, level with V4 in the 5th space, not the 4th.

explain.body: Interpret results against the person's condition and previous results, and act promptly: escalate significant abnormalities to the doctor, document who was told and when. Take samples such as blood cultures before antibiotics are started where possible.

test.q: In hospital, when should blood cultures ideally be taken in relation to starting antibiotics?
options: Before the first antibiotic dose
24 hours after the first dose
At the next routine blood round
After the course has finished
test.why: NICE NG15 rec 1.1.27 advises taking microbiological samples before prescribing antimicrobials in hospital, so cultures can guide treatment; NG253 includes blood culture in the first bloods for high-risk sepsis.

whyNot.1: Cultures taken after antibiotics are more likely to be falsely negative.
whyNot.2: Waiting for a routine round delays both diagnosis and, often, antibiotics.
whyNot.3: Cultures after the course cannot guide the treatment that has already been given.
